newsitem.title: USA: Scientists study first analysis of Martian rock.
newsitem.headline: Scientists study first analysis of Martian rock.

text.p: Space scientists were making last-minute studies of the first robotic analysis of a Martian rock on Tuesday before revealing the results to a waiting world.

The Mars Pathfinder spacecraft's little rover, Sojourner, scanned a crusted rock affectionately named "Barnacle Bill" with its alpha proton X-ray spectrometer for 10 hours, bombarding it with protons and recording the changes in them as they bounced back to the instrument.

The wealth of data gained from the geological experiment late on Sunday was downloaded to computers on Earth and scientists spent much of Monday and Tuesday morning poring over the information. Their findings were to be released at a news briefing later in the day.
The Sojourner performed a similar analysis on Monday on another rock, dubbed "Yogi" because its silhouette resembles a bear, and those results were due to be announced on Wednesday.

Scientists expected the surveys to reveal the composition of the rocks and provide them with insights into how the planet was formed, what changes occurred over billions of years and whether life, however primitive, ever existed there.

The rover was due to complete some different tasks on Tuesday, performing the Martian equivalent of "wheelies" in the fine Martian soil, which one scientist described as having the composition of flour.

The "soil mechanics experiment" involves the rover locking some of its wheels and spinning the remainder to kick up the red soil, and turning in circles so scientists can see, through the images of the track marks, how firm or loose the surface layer is.
Brian Muirhead, the deputy project manager, said the success of the mission astounded him. "I feel like we have won the Superbowl, the World Series and the World Cup," he said.

Matthew Golombek, the mission scientist, said every day brought new surprises from Mars in the form of photographs and data. "We are finding more and more surprises as we look in total at the rocks and the terrain," he said.
One surprise was the amount of evidence indicating a massive, catastrophic flood surged through the Ares Vallis basin where Pathfinder landed, he said.

But that discovery left scientists with another question: What happened to all that water? They also admitted being surprised to find things looked a lot different from high up than from close to the ground.

The Mars lander took the first photographs of the landing site with its camera in a "hunched down" position, then extended it to six feet (two metres) and photographed the same area. "What we thought were big rocks in the first imaging session turned out to be little stones when we got the later photos in," Principal Imaging Investigator Peter Smith said.
